content: Salpingitis is an infection and inflammation of the fallopian tubes. While it is often used interchangeably with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), the term PID is broader and lacks a precise definition. PID can encompass various conditions affecting the female upper genital tract, such as endometritis, oophoritis, myometritis, parametritis, and infections of the pelvic peritoneum. In contrast, salpingitis specifically refers to infection and inflammation confined to the fallopian tubes. The true incidence of salpingitis is likely underestimated due to incomplete and delayed reporting methods. Many cases are only identified after the disease has progressed to the point of causing chronic complications. Among women aged 16 to 25, salpingitis is the most common serious infection, affecting approximately 11% of women of reproductive age. The condition is more prevalent among Black women and those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. However, this disparity is thought to result from factors such as earlier sexual activity, multiple sexual partners, and limited access to adequate healthcare, rather than any inherent risk factor for salpingitis. The highest prevalence of salpingitis is observed in individuals aged 15 to 24, likely due to increased risk associated with multiple sexual partners, reduced awareness of symptoms, and lower likelihood of using contraceptives. There are two forms of salpingitis: acute and chronic. Acute salpingitis causes the fallopian tubes to become red, swollen, and inflamed. The inner walls of the tubes may adhere to one another, leading to obstruction. Additionally, the fallopian tubes can become attached to surrounding structures, such as the intestines. Chronic salpingitis, on the other hand, is less severe and presents with milder symptoms. It often follows an episode of acute salpingitis and tends to persist for a longer duration. Chronic salpingitis may lead to the development of a hydrosalpinx, a condition characterized by fluid accumulation within the fallopian tube. The infection typically originates in the vagina and ascends to the fallopian tubes. Due to the potential for the infection to spread through lymphatic vessels, involvement of one fallopian tube often results in infection of the other. When diagnosing salpingitis, it is essential to differentiate it from other conditions that can cause lower abdominal pain and fever. These include appendicitis, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, cystitis, colorectal cancer, and endometritis.
